summary: Clarifies terms and concepts from RFC 3095, the Robust Header Compression framework. It explains ROHC instances, channels, feedback and contexts, and how they relate to network elements and IP interfaces. It updates RFC 3095 and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3759 clarifies the parts and connections used by Robust Header Compression (ROHC). It explains how compressors, decompressors, channels, feedback, and contexts relate to network elements and IP interfaces.

subtitle: Terms and examples that explain how ROHC components connect across network links.

tldr.problem: RFC 3095 defines Robust Header Compression but some concepts are difficult to relate to network interfaces, links, and management.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines terminology for ROHC instances, channels, feedback, and contexts, and uses link examples to show their relationships.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3759 is an Informational document that updates RFC 3095. It clarifies terminology and relationships; it does not define a new compression protocol.

today: RFC 3759 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 3095. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Terminology Matters
sections.content:
RFC 3095 defines the Robust Header Compression (ROHC) framework and four compression profiles. RFC 3759 says that some concepts in that framework were not described in enough detail to make their relationships clear.

This document adds terminology and examples for ROHC instances, channels, feedback, and contexts. One stated goal is to support and simplify development of the ROHC Management Information Base (MIB).
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC clarifies how ROHC components relate to each other and to the network around them. That shared vocabulary can also help people describe ROHC in management documents.

sections.title: Network Elements, Interfaces, and Links
sections.content:
A network element communicates through one or more IP interfaces. Each IP interface provides an IP-level view of the link technology beneath it. A link may provide one or more logical channels, and those channels may carry data in one direction or both directions.

The RFC gives examples including a one-way satellite link, a two-way point-to-point link such as PPP over a telephone line, a shared Ethernet, and a cellular link with multiple channels. Whether a channel has a return path and whether it is point-to-point affect which forms of header compression can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP interface can use different kinds of links. Some links carry data in one direction, some in both, and some are shared by multiple devices.

sections.title: ROHC Instances and Channels
sections.content:
A ROHC instance performs compression or decompression using one or more ROHC profiles. An instance is either a compressor or a decompressor; even if both exist on one device, they are separate instances.

A ROHC channel always carries compressed packets in one direction from one compressor to one corresponding decompressor. A bidirectional lower-layer link can carry a ROHC channel in each direction. The compressor has three inputs and one output; the decompressor has one input and three outputs.
sections.plainLanguage: A ROHC channel carries compressed packets in one direction, from one compressor to one decompressor. If both devices compress traffic, each direction has its own ROHC channel.

sections.title: How Feedback Returns
sections.content:
A ROHC feedback channel carries information from a decompressor back to its corresponding compressor. It is logically separate from the ROHC channel, although the RFC describes several ways to carry the feedback over the available lower-layer channels.

Feedback may use a dedicated channel, or travel among compressed packets in the opposite direction. Feedback sent as a separate packet among those packets is interspersed; feedback carried inside a compressed packet is piggybacked. Feedback is needed for bidirectional compression.
sections.plainLanguage: A decompressor can send feedback to its compressor. The feedback can use a separate channel or share a channel with compressed packets going the other way.

sections.title: Contexts and Identifiers
sections.content:
A compressor or decompressor can handle multiple concurrent packet streams, subject to a limit. Each stream has a context. Compressed packets carry a context identifier (CID), which tells the decompressor which context applies.

Each ROHC instance has its own context and CID space. The CID space supported by the corresponding decompressor must be at least as large as the compressor's CID space. The RFC summarizes the relationships between network elements, IP interfaces, ROHC instances, channels, and contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: A context stores information for a packet stream. Each compressed packet carries an identifier so the decompressor can select the matching context.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says the split between the general ROHC framework and its profiles is mainly a standardization boundary. An implementation may keep common functions in a framework module and add profile modules, but this is not required by the document.

Understanding how ROHC channels relate to IP interfaces and the physical medium matters for secure use. Because this RFC reviews terminology and definitions, it says it does not add new security issues to the ROHC protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations may organize shared ROHC functions and individual profiles in separate modules. The RFC says its clarification adds no new security issues.

references.text: Bormann, C., et al., "RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Framework and four profiles: RTP, UDP, ESP, and uncompressed", RFC 3095, July 2001.
